segments.description: Welcome, coaches. It's a great privilege to introduce a good mate of mine, Michael Boll, OAM. Michael is the coach of swimmer Emma McKee in Australia's most decorated Olympian and is a former coach of triple gold medalist Stephanie Rice. Michael has been a coach of Australian swimmers who have been on the podium at every summer Olympics between 2008 and the 2020 summer Olympics. Michael, welcome. Thanks, Joe. Pleasure to be here. Yeah, it's good to have you here, too. I'd like to start by offering the opportunity to type in some questions in the chat function below, sorry, in the Q&A section below. So if you'd like to type a message, post it in that and we'll pose those questions to Michael throughout the session. Having no questions, I'll lead off with mine. Winding back to the 80s, you're still a swimmer. You're watching Jono do those crazy laps in the grandstand at Chandler. Then you start your coaching process and you basically ask Terry Cooper to come on as our S&C coach. And then you ask Bob Traffine to do the physioside of it, sorry, not the physiotherapy, but the physical development. He was the first to develop the heart rate monitors. Nowadays, it's taken a step further. Are the athletes of the 80s, 90s, early 2000s any different from the athletes today? How can I say this politically correct? I think the athletes nowadays, I think they're very good, but I think the athletes back in

the 80s and 90s are probably a little bit more robust. I think the athletes these days are a little bit sensitive to some of them, whereas I think the athletes back in the 80s and 90s, you could really, should I use the word bash them about, but really push and drive and they'd come back wanting more now, I think we've got to be a little bit more cautious as a coach in dealing with the kids of post 2000. So all the sport science that goes around, do you think that that's, how has that influenced Has it just refined their skills? Because they're swimming faster than ever, I mean, Emma doing a 50-1-9, that's just madness, isn't it? Well, I think, you know, sports science has definitely helped, like we use sports science on a weekly basis. I think it's probably a thing you can overuse, you know, you can use it too much, definitely, but I think swimming is a very technical sport. It's a driver or a performance shift. So I think, you know, the coaches of the modern era have got to try and use and harness those things that are made available to us. And I think the, you know, the biomechanical stuff that we're doing in the water there has been a big improvement driver for us. I think strength and conditioning is another area that I know particularly with Emma, where we saw big shifts in performance, you know, with that for her. So I think, you know, it's the coach and the sports scientists coming together and coming

up with a plan for each of the individual athletes you've got. You know, there are some athletes that don't respond well to sports science stuff and there are other athletes that crave it. So it's trying to unlock the person in front of you and try and find out what motivates he or she to, you know, to improve and to try and get to that better level. So within your team, so you talked about having the sports scientists, who exactly is part of that team or forms part of that team, including the swimmer? Well, it's a very big group of people. Actually, you've got obviously your physiotherapy, you've got your massage therapy, you've got your biomechanics expert, we've got two of those that work within the confines of our program. There's about 20 swimmers. That's very hard for one person to get through all then. You've got a physiologist, strength conditioning coach, nutritionist, a Pilates lady comes and works with our swimmers two or three times a week. I've got my co-coach, Janelle Palister works with me. So there's a number of different people that go into helping the athletes get better. So do you see yourself as the conductor of all of this orchestra? Well, I think that's the way that you try and do it. I think you don't want too many external people coming in at one time and just overloading the athletes as well. I think that's not a great scenario to be in either. So I think you need to cherry pick who comes in for what sessions and don't overcrowd the

deck with too many people. Have the people that are there that are being effective in trying to get the change or drive the change that you're seeking with the swimmers that you've got. So I think the head coach has got to be in control of that. Your program can't be led by sports science or anyone else. I think you've got to have the vision. I guess it is the vision and the control of the people that are helping you in your program to try and support the athletes that you've got in front of you. And along with the likes of Janelle right now, you've had some incredible assistance over the years with Mick Palfrey, Dean Boxall, who've both gone on to succeed. How are they involved as part of the conversation? Well, I think they're a really integral part of what you're doing because what you're relying on I guess over a period of time is for your assistant coaches to feed athletes through and if they're playing from a different songbook to what you are, you're going to have athletes transition into your program that you've got to reeducate. So I think the coaching staff within your organization, no matter what sport it is, have got to be all on the same page. You've got to have a very similar methodology. Obviously, there's little tweaks and little changes that each individual coach brings to the program, but essentially, I think, you know, we've got to be talking the same language from the intermediate group through to the senior group.

So that transition is seamless once those athletes develop into your senior group. You're hitting the ground running with the people that are coming in. So I spent quite a bit of time, I guess, on the side of the pool while I was coaching, talking to these coaches that were working with the underpinning group, but also once every four weeks, once every six weeks, we'd go out and have a breakey together and just talk about coaching, you know, just shoot the breeze with coaching and talk about philosophy. If they were having any problems within their group and I try and troubleshoot and help to try and, I guess, you know, try and fast track any problems they were having within the programs that they were looking after. You continue that contact now that they're in different spaces, particularly Mick and Dino, do you continue that contact and monitor the performance and still guide them? I wouldn't say so much. I mean, you know, someone like Deans, he's hitting the ground running, you know, he's his own man, he's very, he's very organized and structured with the way he wants to do things. And you'd probably have to ask him what system he's using now. But he often tells me that, you know, obviously the coaches that he trained under, Scott Volker, Steppen Vidbar and myself, have shaped him into the coach that he is today and, you know, good, bad, and ugly, you know, we get on the phone maybe once every month or two

months and not necessarily talking about sessions or sets or anything else, but we're just talking about, you know, just swimming in general, if we're having any problems with kids in the program, just general conversation. And Mick Palfrey, the coach I had before Dean, was probably more about, you know, we'll share sets and training sets and everything else, like Mick loves hearing sets and I like hearing sets from him. Deans probably a little bit more guarded with what he's doing because, you know, we're all coaching simmers that are racing each other at the end of the day. And, you know, he's probably a bit more guarded. Mick would be a little bit more open, but, you know, we certainly have great dialogue. It was great on the Olympic team. There were nine coaches and three of them, myself, Dean and Mick, were all within the same program at one time there. So it was nice to have your two assistant coaches standing alongside you at the Olympics. That was certainly one of the most memorable moments I'll have as a coach. Fantastic. In that environment where you've got people collaborating together, we, I guess, in tennis, we almost suffer a little bit from that isolation, that guarding your own property, your own IP, whatever the case may be. Something was a bit like that prior to Greg introducing the target squads. Can you share a bit about the target squads and how successful they were and have been

and the flow on effect from them? Yeah, I guess the target squad was set up in Queensland originally because New South Wales were kicking out, but, you know, 90% of the Australian team was from New South Wales. So the chairman of Queensland, swimming Greg Lawler, bless his soul, he was in that position for about 30 years and did a magnificent job in getting Queensland going again. And one of the brainchilds that he had back in the 70s was forming the target squad with a vision of trying to get better representation on the Australian swimming team. So what he did was he got all the top coaches into a room. There was Joe King, Laurie Lawrence, John Caloo, Ken Wood, and he sat them round and they came up with the plan to try and get swimming Queensland on the rise again. And one of the things that they did initially, because they didn't have a lot of funding, there were no sponsors that originally came in. So something that was very simple and very cheap was getting all the top players in the city of Queensland. And we'd go Friday, Saturday, Sunday. Can you still hear me, Joe? Yeah. Yeah. We'd go Friday, Saturday, Sunday. We'd just get together and have everyone coach. So all the top coaches would be there with all the top athletes coaching and it was almost like war on water, you know, for about three days, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. All the best sprinters, all the best middle-distance, distance, and as flyers, backstrikes, all came

together for those three days and just absolutely gave it to each other. And I think working together as a group made everyone better and it made Queensland better. And over the period of time, it might have taken six, seven, eight years, just the standard improved. And then the Queensland Academy of Sport came on board with funding and a couple of sponsorships came in. There was, you know, a news power, news agents and there was Forex came on, you know, like a lot of sponsors came on board once that success started to come. Kieran Perkins started Breaking World Records and all of a sudden there was interest. Sponsorship came and then we started going away as a group internationally. There was trips to Japan, the US, Canada, and that just kept lifting the standard. Everyone was aspiring to make that target squad because one of the things that was open to us was international travel, if you got on that target squad, so everyone was really trying hard. That created that competition to try and get on to the target squad. And all of a sudden, you know, over the last probably 15 or 20 years, it's reversed, you know, New South Wales is probably struggling a little bit and Queensland's certainly the dominant force when it comes to swimming in Australia. From what I've seen from the outside in recent years, more importantly, is the relationship between the coaches so amicable and there's no animosity at all between the coaches.

One of the things you said in our little time together in the presentation, you talked about hard working and infectious as two of the key words for you. What is it that you see in the characteristics of the swimmers that make that you catch cry? Well, I think just the success that you've had with the good people, they've been just relentless in their pursuit of meets like the Olympic Games, like the big thing for us is the Olympic Games every four years and that's what we're all measured on. And the athletes that I've had success with at those Olympic Games have been ones that have just been absolutely driven, wouldn't let anything stand in the road of them getting better. And I think you see a lot of people, you know, they come into your program and they'll be great for the first two weeks, that honeymoon period, the first two weeks and all of a sudden reality sinks in and they go back to being like they were when they were in their programs before. But the really good athletes, the driven athletes will find a way to keep lifting the standard of what they're doing in training and when the standard keeps improving in training, it's no surprise that the level that they compete at is at a high level and after doing this for 34 years, it's just time after time after time you see it, you see people who work hard over a long period of time consistently are the ones that stand on top of that podium.

So I guess it's just one of those things that you see through experience, like people can tell you but when you've got athletes like Stephanie and Emma and those sorts of people that are just prepared to do the extra things, like a lot of them talk it but don't walk it, like they say they want to do this, this and this, but when you ask them to come in for an extra session or stay behind for 20 minutes, you know, you get the roll of the eyes, don't worry, it's okay, you go. So I quickly respond, like if someone gives me 90%, I'll give them 70 back, you know, I like an athlete that gives me 100%, you know, that's how I sort of operate, like I'm on a sliding scale, if they give me 90, I give them 70, if they give me 80, I give them 40, nothing less than 80, then I just ignore them a little bit. I think, you know, you've got to give them an opportunity, I don't ignore them, I usually meet with them and I'll say, look, you know, when you came into the program, these were your goals, this is what you told me you wanted to do, you're saying you want to compete at this level but you're delivering and training every day, there's a big yawning gap, you're not going to get to the level you're talking about until I start to see a little bit more from you more consistently in training and I think, you know, those that get it, get it, but those that don't end up maybe going to another program or sort of drifting out

of the sport and I think, you know, the program that I'm in now is very much high performance, it's cruel, it's brutal but I've only got a limited amount of people that I can have in the pool and we've just got to make sure everyone is contributing and, you know, you want people in the program that value ad, you don't want to have people necessarily that are in there bringing that standard down, so I'm very careful with who I take in, you know, you've got to make sure that you're bringing in people into your program, they're coming in fresh, better people that, you know, sort of blue sky thinkers, they, you know, they want to, you know, they want to do, they don't just want to talk about it, they want to actually do it, so I think that's important to the group and I know after the Olympics we had four or five, six people come in, a couple of young guys, Mack Hortons and older guy, 25, very disappointed with how he went last year at the Olympics and, you know, disappointed with, you know, sitting in general over the last 12 months, he had a great relationship with his coach, Craig Jackson, but just felt he needed a change and him and I spoke at length about, you know, what did it look like him coming in and he said, no, I'm ready to try something different and something new, you tell me what to do and I'll do it and that's, that's the attitude that you want to kind of have in there, you don't want

someone, he's won an Olympic gold medal, but he's never sat down with me in the four months he's been there and said, Bali, I don't think I'm doing enough of this or I think I need to do more of this, he's putting his trust and his faith in what you're saying, so like the buy-in from him is 100% and I'll certainly be trying to do my, you know, very best to get him back up to the level that he was at before. Or even better. Or better. Yeah. We've had a question in here from Brad, is it important when deciding your coaching personnel in a high performance coaching team to get experienced coaches that have had special skill sets or have a developmental coach and upskill them? Cool, it's a good question. I think both are good, provided the person with experience is going to do what you sort of think is the right thing, like if you're getting an older person coming into your program who doesn't believe in your philosophies or doesn't want to do it the way that you want to do it, I think you're going to set your program back five years. So I'd look at if that older person coming in with a lot of experience had an open mind and thought you were a great coach and your program was good and everything else, there's not an issue. But if you've got an older coach coming in and in the background he's wide-adding, you know, what your philosophies are, he's going to create more problems than not.

A young development coach is fantastic. I think once again the same thing, you've got to have that young development person coming in not pushing their philosophies on to you, they've got to be very respectful of what you're doing and then after a period of time, you as a young developing coach, you sit down with that older coach, he's your boss and you say, look, I wouldn't mind doing this with the younger guys, but this amount of time, what do you reckon? You work that consultative approach, but you don't want an older person coming in telling you to throw everything out and a younger person coming in telling you what you're doing is hopeless. You need harmony within your workplace and I insist on that with the people I have working with me, like Mick Palafry and Dean Boxer were two of my former slimmers, so they were very aware of my style and how I did it and all that sort of stuff, so there was no drama. Whereas I think if you're getting people in here you don't know much about, I think you as the employer need to be very thoughtful and very careful with the start that you select because you can throw your program back very quickly if you've got people that aren't working on the same team as you, so my advice is either way, whether it's an older one or a younger one, just make sure that they're willing to listen to what you want, that you don't want people telling you what to do.

And it also goes to the investment that you're putting into the other person because if you can't give them the time or the opportunity to voice their opinions and to learn from you, those relationships can sell pretty quickly as well. We've had another question here from Paul. Fantastic presentation Michael, really enjoying it. What do you think the next frontier is in athlete or coach development and coach development and do we all just have to get better at the basics? Fantastic presentation Michael, really enjoying it. What do you think the next frontier is, athlete and coach development, question mark, or do we all just have to get better at the basics? I think it's a combination of everything. I think in my opinion, like the communication between the coach and the athlete is one of the most important things, like every successful athlete I've seen, whether it's in football or in tennis or in swimming or in any sport, they've had that mentor that's helped them. I think when you think of Wayne Bennett and Darren Lock here, that relationship there, Elfin Langer and Wayne Bennett. Like I think there's just so many examples you can think of of people who have been excellent, who have had that mentor above them that has really led their changes that they've had to make. So I think that just an establishment of a great relationship between you as the coach and the athletes that you've got in your program is very important.

I think with the older athletes, one of the big things that I'm all at the moment is the recovery part of it, but we work in swimming with a fair bit of intensity. And as the athletes in my program are getting older, I need to be more upskilled with the areas of recovery. Like Emily Seabomb at 29 can't train the way she did when she was 16. So if I try and coach her like a 16-year-old, I'm going to end up with an athlete who will be burnt out. So it's us as coaches upskilling and trying to find about, if you've got challenges within your coaching program with older athletes, injured athletes, athletes that are non-responsive, people that maybe aren't eating properly and aren't recovering properly so they can't train properly. Like looking at all those little extra things, I think are some of the little two or three percent things that go to making a big difference to your program. I've tended to use, I think as I've coached more, I used to try and do everything myself. I used to do the gym, the stroke correction, this, that, that. And I found that I was probably missing a lot. So I think having people within your coaching framework as well, like we mentioned, before all those extra people that work with us, the physios, the biomechanics people, etc., having those people come in, you've got to have a great relationship and trust with them. But you've got to give them the ability to be able to action change.

You know, biomechanics, I'm reasonable at it, but there are people within our program that are doctors of biomechanics that are a lot more well versed than I am. So I've got to allow them to be able to try and help the people I've got. So I try and be an active part of the change where I listen to what that person is saying to the athletes, but you know, they're probably better positioned to make those changes in consultation with me as the coach, that they can see things that maybe I can't. So I'm not silly enough to think that I know everything. I think being able to utilize the experts that are around you in all areas can help make you a little bit more of a rounded coach. Excellent. And seeking out that advice and guidance is always important because as you say, you can't do where all the hats that go into being a swimming coach. The same thing for tennis coach as well. In terms of programming, tennis, we have a series of tournaments throughout the year and we have bigger tournaments, some bigger than others. But for you, you're gearing up for one day in four years time. How does the periodization and the programming work? Is it a very complex and still has to be adaptable or is it a certain milestones that you need to reach at certain times? Well, I think it sort of varies and differs with the athletes that you've gotten your program, like Emma McCann's getting to the end of a career potentially. I don't want to wish

her to retire very soon. She's 27 years of age and she's not going to swim forever. So bearing that in mind, we've got two and a half years to the next Olympics. It'd be silly of me to get her in and force a result the next six months because I think I kind of look at the major meat that we're working towards. And for her, it's Paris 2024 and I work backwards from there. So for her to be in the best shape in Paris, in my opinion, she's going to take a little bit of a break which she's having at the moment. She won't start back till February. She's going to bypass the world championships that are in Japan this year. The trials for those are in 10 weeks. So we've just taken her out of the equation for that. She'll potentially swim at the Commonwealth Games. So I think it's coming up with the plan for the individuals that you've got in your program to get them over the line at the meat that you're working towards. So with her, it's a very steady first six months of the year this year and then the back six months will be a little bit more pressure on her with Commonwealth Games. There's a competition, international competition called the ISL. She'll swim in that. She'll swim in the FINA World Cups, which are money-making events. So she'll back end this year. The last six months will be solid. The first six months, it's just laying the foundations again. So in swimming, we talk about, if you look at the

season, just establishing a good aerobic base, making sure there are aerobic conditioning workers done really well. You're not cutting any corners. You're getting them in good physical shape, both in the gym and in the pool. And then once they've established that good aerobic base, starting to put into place some race preparation sessions and sets within the program. So if you're looking at a 16-week block of work, the first six or seven weeks might be developing that aerobic base. Once they've established that aerobic base, maintaining the aerobic, but the focus shifts to doing more quality-based, race-paced type stuff in training. And then we normally just taper them down at the end for about two weeks, generally speaking, at the end. So base work into quality work, into tapering, into racing. And we normally, you know, if you look at the calendar year, our trials are traditionally in about June. This year they're going to be in April, but normally they're in June. So the trials would be their first rest, but I've got to swim fast at the Olympic trials or at the World Trials. And then normally that benchmark meet, whether it's the Worlds or the Olympic Games, is about four to five weeks after our trial. So you're looking at kind of double taping them, double tapering them, getting them to swim quite fast at the trials. But then hopefully four or five weeks later, getting into peak up and get to a high peak at that major benchmark competition.

And after that, I'll have a break for a week or two, and then I'll start them all rolling again with the next thing that's coming up. And that change in the tapering has, because of the time length between trials and games, has changed. We've sort of followed the Americans on that one. And it's been, well, from Tokyo, seen fairly successful. Yeah, it was. Like what we used to do is we used to have our trials in March and then the Olympics were in July. So there was that three month period in between. And because that three month period is winter, there's not a lot of competitions and that thing or that, you know, competitions or racing opportunities for our athletes. So what they decided to do was push the trials a little bit later and have them in June about four weeks before the Olympics. And they set up structured competitions that help get the sinners ready for the trials. So as you said, Joe, they follow the American concept, the way that they do it. And it seems to have worked quite successfully. I mean, having that smaller amount of time, that four or five week period between the trials and the actual games, like there were a lot more people. What we look at are people that swim at this level of trials and try and get an improvement. And I think there was something like 70% of the athletes improved their performances from the trials to the actual Olympics. Whereas before, in Rio, it might have been 25% or 30%

of the athletes improved their performance with that three month break in between. So I think it's something that we've looked at very closely. Juck over on and our former coach brought it in and Rowan Taylor, our current head coach, has decided to keep it going. Yeah. Great learnings from lessons from performances that weren't quite ideal, hey? Yeah, definitely. Now, unfortunately, time is running out. But we can't let you go before you give us your three tips for coaches, or your top tips for coaches who are studying out on their journey. Yeah. Tough one. I think the first one's patience. Don't be in a hurry. I think that's one of the things that I've learned very much over the time that I've been doing it. You know, like you see a lot of people, especially younger coaches, coming in and want to be the world's best coach in the first two years that they want it quick and fast. And I think there's no shortcuts. So I think you've got to be very patient with yourself, but very patient with your athletes that you're working with. I think you've got to be a student of your sport. You need to be watching a lot of video and listening to people that have been around for a long time and learning. You might listen to a tennis coach, for example, that is a guru and 90% of what he says is great, but there's 10% you just block your ears to that you don't like. But I think that 90% is the stuff you've got to focus in on. So I think you've got to feel like you're ever learning. There

was an older coach we had in swimming, Joe King. Joe, I remember him. He was on the Olympic team in 92. He was about 84, 85 years of age, very old guy. And when we did our level one coaching courses, he'd sit in the front row and he'd always be there the lecture before he was speaking. He spoke and then he'd stay for the lecture directly after. I said, Mr King, you don't have to stay for all this. He said, son, you're never too old to learn. If I pick up one thing from him and one thing from her when they're talking, I'll be a happy man when I leave here. So I think, you know, me as a younger coach listening to someone like him, who was one of my heroes as a young developing coach, I think that's how I've kind of taken a fit from what he said there. So I think, you know, never stop learning. The first thing I said, I think it was patience. And I think, you know, perseverance is probably the other one. I think, you know, there were periods of time there where I felt like I was going well in coaching and everything was going nice. We had representatives in 92, 96. The 2000 Olympics, which was the home Olympics in Sydney, I had no one from my team that was Australian, maybe Olympic team. And I thought, you know, I wasn't sure if I wanted to keep going. I'd started out doing physical education. I thought, oh, maybe, you know, I'll, you know, go and be a PE teacher like my wife's a PE teacher. Because it was a horrible feeling not having anyone

on that Sydney Olympic team. But I think, you know, I just thought, no, no, you know, I'm still enjoying it. That was a little bit of short term pain. It was a real snack between the eyes for me. But I think that has been the thing that feeling in 2000, that's probably set me up for the good thing. I've been lucky enough to have the good success over the last four or five cycles was that horrible disappointment. You know, I think if you persevere as an athlete or as a coach or anything in life, I think if you, you know, if you stick at it, stick to the task, you'll be successful in the end. So that's the third one. Great messages, mate. Great messages. And that brings us to an end. But if you'd like the opportunity to have some one on one time with Foley, please fill out the survey monkey that will be sent out at the end of the conference. So Michael, once again, thanks very much, mate. It's been an absolute pleasure. Pleasure, Joe. Happy to help. Good luck, everyone.
